Minimum CCP required for downvoting

Maybe, but probably not. The current traveling through water will fall off with distance, so the closer you are to the toaster the higher it will be. Since humans are made up of mostly water, you'll be very close to as conductive as the water is. In a semi-related example, when lightning strikes water, the current travels along the surface of the water (due to it acting as a Faraday Cage), being lethal for ~20ft. Obviously toasters have a way lower voltage than the average lightning strike, so the lethal range would be much smaller.

Water itself isn't very conductive, but pool water usually contains a lot of chlorine, which makes it much more conductive. A similar principle applies to the human body, although it is much less water by composition. The human body is fairly resistive from the outside when dry, roughly 2-2.5 orders of magnitude more than when wet. Unfortunately exact computation is complicated since both the pool and humans are 3-dimensional systems, and different parts of the body react differently to electric current.

The current density will be (roughly) inversely proportional to the distance of the source (toaster). So, in a perfectly conducting fluid, you would feel, say, 20 amps at 1 meters distance, 10A @ 2m, 5A @ 4m and so on. The conductivity is dependent on the amount of solutes in the pool water.
